excerpt: Statsig is an experimentation, feature flag and product analytics platform. OpenAI bought it in 2025 for $1.1 billion; Amplitude acquired the product in May 2026.
content:
Statsig is a product development platform for running A/B tests and experiments, managing feature flags, product and web analytics, and session replays. Engineering and product teams use it to roll features out gradually, measure their effect on metrics and decide what to keep. Its pricing page says about 90% of its customers use it for free.

Statsig was founded by Vijaye Raji and is based in the Seattle area. In September 2025 OpenAI agreed to buy it in an all-stock deal worth $1.1 billion, a figure an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch and which GeekWire said matched Statsig's valuation in a funding round that May. OpenAI was already a customer. Raji became OpenAI's CTO of Applications, overseeing product engineering for ChatGPT and Codex. Statsig then has a further chapter: a note added to its acquisition blog post says that Amplitude acquired Statsig on 5 May 2026. The original team stayed at OpenAI, while the product, brand and customers became part of Amplitude, and Statsig's homepage now describes it as part of the Amplitude family.

Statsig publishes its prices. The Developer plan is free and includes 2 million events a month and 50,000 session replays. Pro costs $150 a month with 5 million events included and $0.05 per 1,000 events after that, and Enterprise is quoted. Feature flag checks are unlimited on every plan. That makes it easy to try against rivals such as LaunchDarkly, Optimizely, PostHog and Amplitude's own experiment tools.

We have not used Statsig for this page. It brings together Statsig's own website and the reporting linked under Sources, and says where each fact comes from. Nothing here is paid placement.

use_cases: Running A/B tests and measuring their effect on metrics
Rolling out features gradually with feature flags
Watching session replays to see how users behave
Turning a feature off quickly if it causes problems

fit: product and engineering teams that ship often and want to measure each change
startups that need a generous free tier
companies with high event volumes that want usage-based pricing
not_fit: teams that only need simple website analytics
buyers wary of a product that has changed owners twice in a year
